title: Physics-informed Neural Networks Based on the Fokker-Planck Model for Rarefied Gas Flows
summary: Rarefied nonequilibrium flows are described by the Boltzmann equation, which can be solved using stochastic particle or deterministic methods. With advances in computing, data-assisted physics-informed neural networks have been widely used for flow prediction by combining governing equations with measured or computed data. Data-free PINNs do not require such training data and have been widely studied for continuum flows, but their application to rarefied flows remains limited. This study develops a data-free Fokker-Planck physics-informed neural network (FP-PINN) to describe rarefied nonequilibrium flows. The physics loss is constructed from the ellipsoidal statistical Fokker-Planck (ES-FP) equation using a velocity distribution function (VDF) closure and moment projection. The FP-PINN is evaluated for a steady one-dimensional Mach 10 normal shock. The FP-PINN results agree with the numerical ES-FP results, with errors below $1\%$. Compared with the particle ES-FP results, the FP-PINN predicts a sharper shock structure with errors up to $17\%$. This difference is attributed to the VDF closure and moment projection.

title: Thermo-viscous feedback in heat transport through fracture-matrix systems with finite thermal capacity
comment: 67 pages, 11 figures. Revised manuscript submitted to Advances in Water Resources. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23301912
summary: In geothermal systems, injected fluid flows along preferential fracture pathways and exchanges heat with matrix blocks. Reduced models often neglect temperature-dependent viscosity and assume unlimited matrix storage, although the thermal capacity accessible to the flow is finite. This work analyzes thermo-viscous feedback in a planar fracture-matrix system where viscosity controls discharge through the integrated hydraulic resistance, while finite capacity enters through an effective single-timescale memory fixed by initial uptake and total capacity. The reduced model gives parsimonious semi-analytical predictions with physically based parameters, verified against the nonlinear solution. A perturbation hierarchy separates matrix storage from the hydraulic response it induces, while an exponential velocity reconstruction preserves the exact terminal discharge and bounds front-moment errors within the front-moment limit model. At fixed pressure difference, heating accelerates and broadens the front, whereas cooling delays and sharpens it. The terminal discharge depends only on the endpoint viscosity ratio, while matrix uptake, storage and contrast determine its approach time. At fixed rate, viscosity alters only the pressure drop, not the thermal response. Finite thickness controls the transition to capacity-limited equilibration, and strong matrix uptake collapses the isoviscous response onto a two-variable similarity surface.

title: SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE: High-performance finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov-exponent computations for CPUs and GPUs
summary: Finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov exponents (FTLE and FSLE) characterise material stretching and transport barriers over prescribed time intervals and separation scales, but their evaluation from three-dimensional velocity sequences requires large computational costs. We introduce SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE, two modules of StreamCenter+ for CPU- and GPU-accelerated Lagrangian analysis. The modules support structured and native unstructured meshes, selectable integration and interpolation schemes, and graphical and command-line workflows. Rolling snapshot reuse, memory-bounded FTLE batching, device-resident trajectory state and active-set FSLE advancement reduce data movement and redundant computation, achieving the state-of-the-art (SOTA) computational performance among peer packages. For a billion-seed benchmark, strong-scaling efficiencies on 32 GPUs reach 86.3% for FTLE and 95.2% for FSLE. FTLE is verified with published steady and unsteady Arnold-Beltrami-Childress (ABC) flows and stationary concentrated vortex model (SCVM), while FSLE is verified in linear stretching and rotational shear flows. As examples, applications reveal the spanwise reorganisation of stretching layers in a shear-thinning lid-driven cavity, and resolve three-dimensional stretching structures associated with contrasting tracer dispersion around an urban building canopy at NUS campus. These results demonstrate a scalable workflow in large-scale Lagrangian diagnostics and analysis of flow data.

title: Pair-exchange dynamics of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence
summary: Nonlinear interactions in incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) and Navier-Stokes turbulence involve three spatial fluctuations conservatively exchanging, e.g., energy. The mathematical structure of a triad interaction does not allow to unambigously determine the specific contribution of each of the participating fluctuations to the resulting exchanges. Presently, only additional assumptions allow for the deconstruction of triad interactions into a sum of pair exchanges. This work proves that in incompressible MHD the simultaneous nonlinear transfer of cross-helicity sufficiently constrains the triad dynamics such that a mathematically unique pair-exchange representation of nonlinear energy and cross-helicity transfer is possible.

title: Implementing the EIT complete electrode model through Robin boundary conditions
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures; supplementary material: 24 pages, 3 figures. Code and reproduction package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23239050
summary: Objective. Medical electrical impedance tomography systems prescribe electrode currents. Accurate voltages, even on passive electrodes, require the complete electrode model (CEM), the most accurate model known for skin electrodes. Its current constraints specify total electrode currents, whereas standard finite element boundary interfaces impose local conditions. We describe how to implement the CEM through Robin boundary conditions, which are available in standard FEM packages. Approach. Prescribed electrode potentials give Robin problems whose unit-potential responses define an electrode transadmittance matrix. We prove equivalence to the conventional augmented CEM and formalise the discrete energy, equivalence and reference arguments in Lean 4. Numerical comparisons use two-dimensional P1 finite elements in DOLFINx, FreeFEM, GetFEM, MFEM and NGSolve, with the same nodal reference potential as EIDORS. Main results. For identical assembled blocks, the two procedures have the same solution set whenever the Robin matrix is invertible. Across the five packages in dimensionless test cases, maximum absolute electrode-potential differences from EIDORS were below $5\times10^{-13}$ (2692 nodes), and errors against an exact rational-arithmetic reference were below $1.1\times10^{-13}$ (2535 nodes). Significance. Standard Robin solves and consistent electrode-current integration provide a portable route to the current-driven CEM, with current constraints enforced through a small electrode system.

title: Evolutionary Informed Translation from Protein to Nucleic Acid Sequence
summary: The choice of nucleic acid sequence for a given protein strongly impacts function and is species-specific. Current protein-to-nucleic-acid translation models treat sequences in isolation, often over-favoring frequently used codons. To generate more natural nucleic acid sequences, we introduce PINATA (Phylogenetically Informed protein to Nucleic Acid Translation with sequence Alignment), a model that leverages sequences from related species encoded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to guide prediction. Our architecture leverages evolutionary context and learns species-and protein specific context to make biologically-informed predictions. Evaluated across 61,934 gene trees and 882 species, PINATA generates sequences that mirror the naturally-occurring sequence substantially better than existing language models. PINATA leverages MSA data to improve exact native codon recovery by 17.95 percentage points over existing language models, effectively preserves natural rare-codon nuances, and more closely matches native sequence properties. PINATA maintains strong predictive performance even with limited evolutionary data. While previous methods largely treated sequences from different species in isolation, our method leverages the evolutionary relationships between nucleic acids and proteins across species to create a more biologically-informed translation. We demonstrate that leveraging rich evolutionary data through an biologically-designed method strongly aids in translating protein sequences to nucleic acid sequences across species. We will make data and code publicly available upon publication.

title: The typical red cell makes too little vacuole material for coalescence to build the large vacuoles of pocked cells
comment: 70 pages, 8 figures; Supplementary Materials included (pages 36-70, 2 figures, 28 tables); Movies S1 and S2 are ancillary files. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Red blood cells carrying intracellular vacuoles, called pocked cells, are a sensitive marker of splenic function: about 0.5% of cells in healthy people, 20 to 70% after splenectomy. Vacuoles too small to see are common, and visible ones are thought to grow when small ones merge. We tested that idea with a particle model that resolves the cell's membrane, its contents and every vacuole, and with an inventory of the vacuole volume a cell can make. In tube, shear and vascular flows, a cell's vacuoles met within a second, and, allowed to fuse, ten merged into one to five. Meeting is not what limits growth; material is. At the rate measured after splenectomy, all the vacuoles an average cell makes in its 120-day life fuse into one body 0.6 $μ$m across, the size healthy cells carry, but 16 times smaller in volume than the 1.5-$μ$m bodies of patients without a spleen. Taking vacuole size as set at formation, a population model in which vacuoles are made mainly in young cells, and far faster in a small minority that alone makes material for a large one, accounts for the published counts, sizes and age profiles and, on first-hand measurements, favours a splenic clearance that rises several-fold as cells age; letting that minority's vacuoles fuse fits nearly as well. At a model splenic slit, the cell's spare surface decided passage, and a vacuole mattered only when it led. A slit experiment would test whether brief encounters fuse vacuoles.

title: napari-TurboBox: Interactive Multi-Viewer Bounding Box Annotation for AI-Guided Volumetric Bioimaging
summary:
Promptable segmentation models turn one 3D bounding box into an instance mask. Box placement therefore limits how fast microscopy volumes with thousands of objects are annotated. Each box must be checked in several synchronized viewers, but napari-bbox shares no state between viewers. An edit must update every viewer and slows down with more boxes. napari-TurboBox instead holds one shared copy of the boxes for all viewers. In a four-viewer layout, napari-TurboBox needs a few milliseconds per mouse move to update the three slice viewers up to $10^4$ boxes. The same update in napari-bbox leaves the 33 ms budget beyond about $10^3$ boxes and takes 159 ms at $10^4$. Boxes stay axis-aligned and export to COCO and YOLO as per-slice 2D boxes.
  napari-TurboBox is a pure-Python plugin for napari 0.6.6 to 0.9. The code is available at https://github.com/N-Friederich/napari-turbobox under the Apache 2.0 licence, and version 0.1.0 is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23090828 on Zenodo.

title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements becomes particularly challenging when data are completely absent from dynamically critical regions, such as the vortex-formation region of a wake. Conventional interpolation and numerical reconstruction methods generally require sufficient spatial or boundary information, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can also face difficulties when sparse and noisy observations provide little or no supervision in the region of interest. To address this gap, we propose a Fourier-feature-embedded complex-valued physics-informed convolutional residual network (FCV-PICRN) for sparse, gappy, and noisy flow-field reconstruction. The framework integrates Fourier features for oscillatory and multiscale structures, complex-valued representations for coupled amplitude--phase learning, and convolutional residual blocks constrained by the Navier--Stokes equations. The method is first verified using the Taylor--Green vortex at $Re=100$ and then evaluated for the cylinder wake at $Re=100$. Three severe missing-data configurations are imposed in the dynamically sensitive wake: a large hole, a large truncation, and a plus-shaped gap extending in both streamwise and transverse directions. These gaps are further combined with additive Gaussian and multiplicative speckle noise. Despite having no supervised velocity data inside the excluded regions, FCV-PICRN reconstructs velocity, pressure, and vorticity with high structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and remains robust under Gaussian noise up to $20\%$. Finally, for forced two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence with $5\%$ Gaussian noise, FCV-PICRN yields lower reconstruction errors than a conventional PINN. These results demonstrate robust physics-informed reconstruction of severely incomplete and noisy flows across laminar and turbulent regimes.

title: Attenuation corrected activity reconstruction for listmode TOF-PET data
summary: Time-of-flight (TOF) positron emission tomography (PET) emission data allow joint estimation of the activity and attenuation images. The methods proposed so far rely on reconstructions from TOF histograms of the measurements. However, with the rapid data increase of total-body (TB) scanners and the ever improving TOF and intrinsic resolutions, more memory and computation efficient techniques for joint reconstruction need to be developed. In this work, a modified version of the maximum likelihood activity and attenuation correction factors algorithm (MLACF) is presented, that jointly estimates the activity image together with the attenuation factors (AFs) from listmode emission data. The method does not require TOF histogramming of the data, however it still relies on a coarsely sampled (i.e. mashed) non-TOF histogram of the emission data. The activity distribution is subsequently quantified by reconstructing and enforcing known expected tissue attenuation on an attenuation reconstruction from the estimated AF values. The algorithm is evaluated using 3D simulations as well as clinical TOF-PET measurements of a patient scan and compared to reference reconstructions. As could be expected, we find the reconstruction accuracies improve with an "optimal" histogramming of the TOF emission data, increasing the signal to noise ratio of the data used for joint estimation. With an "optimal" histogramming of the measurements, the attenuation corrected activity distributions from TOF emission data only are comparable to the gold-standard in PET/CT.

title: Multiscale Quantum-Classical Simulation of Protein Autoproteolysis in a Million-Atom Membrane Environment
summary: Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.

title: Deep Learning for Forest Plantation Mapping in Godavari Districts of Andhra Pradesh, India
summary: Small-area forest plantations play a vital role in the socioeconomic well-being of farmers in Southeast Asia. Most plantations are established on former agricultural land, often on land less suitable for agriculture. Plantations that are converted from natural forest have adverse impacts on biodiversity. Mapping small-area plantations is thus important to understand the dynamics of forest cover in Southeast Asia and to study the social, economic, and ecological effects of this important land cover and land use change. While the small size of forest plantations makes it difficult to detect them using moderate resolution satellite sensors, the problem is exacerbated by the high degree of mixing between plantations, surrounding vegetation, and other land covers, which often show variegated responses in satellite signals across space and time. In this paper, we study the problem of mapping small-area forest plantations in East and West Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, India using deep learning methods. Remotely sensed cloud-free data from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 S10 product were classified using a pixel-level neural network and training data labeled using a field-based survey in concert with expert aerial photo interpretation. We compare the performance of deep learning methods with a baseline random forest classifier in our study region of 21543 sq. km over a period of 3 years and analyze the differences in the results across land cover classes and seasons.

title: Azimuthal Instability in Oscillating Liquid Jets by the Weber Number Variations
comment: The following article has been submitted to Physics of Fluids
summary: This paper investigates the dependence of azimuthal mode growth rate of oscillating liquid laminar jets on the Weber number. The oscillating liquid laminar jets were simulated over a range of Weber numbers. The simulation setup was validated by comparing the instantaneous interface shapes and the visible azimuthal mode from experimental measurements. As the Weber number increases, the spreading angle rises due to the small surface tension, and higher azimuthal modes are observed. Fourier Transform analysis is used to find the exact azimuthal mode of the simulation results. The dominant azimuthal mode increases as the Weber number increases. A power-law dependence of the growth rate on the Weber number is identified, with the obtained exponents showing good agreement with linear instability analysis. Furthermore, the rescaled Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) results collapse onto a single growth curve for each azimuthal mode, validating the proposed power-law for predicting the growth rates of oscillating liquid jets.

title: Localizing and quantifying cerebral arterial stenosis from sparse velocity waveforms using a conditional neural operator
summary: Cerebral arterial stenosis alters blood flow throughout the vascular network, complicating the estimation of its location and severity from sparse velocity observations. We developed a conditional neural operator that predicts cerebral hemodynamics for candidate stenoses and enables inverse estimation through waveform comparison. Training data were generated using a sequential 0D-1D model that simulates pressure, cross-sectional area, and velocity under varying anatomical, physiological, and stenosis conditions. The operator encodes a single stenosis within vessel tokens and uses global attention to represent its effects across the network. Severity-gated coupling connects these representations to a shared field decoder, while paired healthy simulations constrain baseline predictions. After training, model weights remain fixed, and stenosis location and severity are estimated by minimizing the mismatch between predicted and observed midpoint velocity waveforms. Network-averaged relative validation errors were 0.14% for pressure, 0.59% for area, and 2.79% for velocity. For an eight-vessel observation configuration, localization accuracy across 20 candidate vessels was 99.4% without added noise and 96.0% at the 30% noise setting. Comparisons between configurations with equal numbers of observed vessels showed that measurement placement influenced recovery. Errors and localization ambiguities were greater in selected communicating and distal arteries. These results demonstrate the feasibility of surrogate-based stenosis estimation in simulated cerebral networks and highlight the importance of observation placement. Evaluation was limited to unseen stenosis scenarios within sampled anatomical and physiological conditions. Generalization to new individuals and clinical measurements requires further investigation.

title: CRUX: Clinical-Text Anchoring for Cross-Institutional CT-Pathology Fusion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Survival Prediction
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Preprint. Extended version of a MICCAI 2024 paper (Kim et al., 2024)
summary: Accurate prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) benefits from integrating computed tomography (CT) and histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), which capture complementary macroscopic and microscopic disease characteristics. Fusing these modalities is difficult: their features come from different pretrained foundation-model encoders and lack spatial correspondence, and both are sensitive to institution-specific acquisition and staining, causing multimodal models to overfit site-specific artifacts and generalize poorly. We present CRUX (CRoss-modal Unification via teXt anchoring), a fusion framework that uses clinical text---encoded by a biomedical language model---as an institution-invariant semantic anchor. Because clinical variables follow standardized classification systems, their embeddings occupy a representation space that is consistent across institutions, providing a stable reference frame for aligning heterogeneous imaging features. CRUX introduces a text-mediated cross-modal bridge in which CT- and pathology-derived text-query summaries exchange information within a compact text semantic space through a learnable hub token, avoiding direct image-space cross-attention that would propagate domain-specific artifacts. We evaluate on 2,157 NSCLC patients from five hospitals, holding out one hospital (N=446) entirely for external validation. CRUX attains an external concordance index (C-index) of 0.761, the highest among all unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal configurations. Notably, direct CT-WSI fusion degrades under distribution shift, whereas text anchoring restores and improves cross-institutional generalization. These results indicate that language-model-encoded clinical text is an effective structured prior for robust, generalizable multimodal cancer prognosis.

title: Streamwise dispersion with interphase mass transfer through a tube
summary: Reactive solute transport in shear flows is of broad importance in chemical engineering, liquid--solid chromatography, and environmental mechanics, particularly in flow reactors and fluidic devices involving interphase mass transfer. Based on the recently developed streamwise dispersion theory for inert solutions (Guan & Chen, 2024, J. Fluid Mech., vol. 980, A33), we present an analytical model for reactive dispersion of chemically active solutes characterized by first-order, irreversible surface reactions. The extension is not a simple perturbation because the reactive boundary destroys mass conservation with streamwise and radial derivatives coupled. The model establishes how the microscopic kinetic reactivity and radial eigenmodes combine to determine a newly defined (effective) local exchange rate. We derive rigorous explicit solutions for the local moments, concentration, and phenomenological transport coefficients at arbitrary reactivity, in quantitative agreement with numerical simulations across all regimes. For tube Poiseuille flows, we reveal pre-asymptotic behaviours including sign-changing radial exchange, reactivity-enhanced drift, reactivity-reduced dispersivity, and non-Gaussian concentration profiles. Small- and large-Damköhler-number asymptotics for the local and global transport coefficients identify the reaction-limited and diffusion-limited regimes, connecting the conservative case to the Dirichlet limit at infinite reactivity. This streamwise perspective could advance our understanding of macroscale transport in chemically active systems.

title: Deep Learning Reconstruction for Accelerated Radial CEST MR Fingerprinting
summary:
Purpose: To accelerate chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance fingerprinting (CEST-MRF) using temporal deep learning reconstruction.
  Methods: Ten healthy volunteers underwent repeated test-retest golden-angle radial CEST-MRF acquisitions with 30 measurements and 34 spokes per measurement. The Movienet network was adapted to reconstruct accelerated radial CEST-MRF data. Separate models were trained using 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 20, and 34 spokes per measurement. Temporal and coil correlations were exploited by concatenating time and coil dimensions in the input. GRASP-based locally low-rank (GRASP-LLR) reconstruction was used for comparison. Quantitative DRONE fitting generated tissue parameter maps. Movienet-8 was evaluated with leave-one-subject-out analysis. Prospectively acquired 8-spoke datasets were compared with paired 34-spoke acquisitions, and Movienet-8 and Movienet-34 were compared with a 64-spoke acquisition.
  Results: In the held-out retrospective series, median Pearson correlations between Movienet and GRASP-LLR were 0.795, 0.947, 0.974, 0.977, and 0.981 for 1, 8, 16, 20, and 34 spokes, respectively. Corresponding NRMSE values were 14.7, 8.2, 5.9, 5.3, and 5.1 percent. Across 10 leave-one-subject-out volunteers, median image correlation was 0.965 and NRMSE was 7.5 percent. Reconstruction of a 30-slice series required 1.7 s with Movienet versus approximately 45 min with GRASP-LLR.
  Conclusion: Movienet enables whole-brain radial CEST-MRF acquisition in 3 min, with image reconstruction in less than 2 s.

title: End-to-End Learned Image Coding: From Rate-Distortion Optimization to Practical Deployment
summary: End-to-end learned image coding (LIC) has achieved substantial improvements in rate--distortion (R--D) performance, yet practical deployment requires addressing a broader set of system-level constraints. This article provides a deployment-oriented review of LIC, with particular attention to the transition from high-performance neural compression models to practical codecs. We first summarize the basic end-to-end coding framework, including learned transforms, quantization, entropy modeling, and R--D optimization. We then review practical extensions that are increasingly important for deployment, including variable-rate coding and rate control, integer-precision inference and cross-platform consistency, robustness and communication resilience, lightweight and hardware-aware implementation, and standardization and interoperability. To study these issues under a common setting, we further introduce TinyLIC as an open benchmark and reproducible case study for rate--distortion--complexity analysis. Experimental results illustrate the trade-offs among compression efficiency, computational complexity, numerical consistency, and robustness. In particular, TinyLIC with approximately 10 KMACs/pixel decoding complexity substantially outperforms the H.265/HEVC image-profile anchor on Kodak, while the 50 KMACs/pixel configuration achieves performance comparable to the H.266/VVC image-profile anchor on several test sets. The review highlights practical constraints and design trade-offs that remain central to the deployment and interoperability of learned image codecs. Materials are accessible at https://njuvision.github.io/TinyLIC.

title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades
summary: The impact of droplets, such as rain and sea sprays, on wind turbine blade surfaces can cause severe damage through leading-edge erosion (LEE). Current industrial practice has largely relied on empirical fatigue models to predict damage progression and guide maintenance. However, an important limitation of existing models is the assumption on ideal impact conditions, including perfectly spherical droplet and normal incidence, which rarely occur in reality. This study develops a fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model that couples incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element (FE) analysis of blade materials. Using this framework, we investigate the impact dynamics of droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations. The results reveal a positive correlation between the peak impact pressure, the influential area at the pressure peak, and the peak impact force. In contrast, the time of peak force scales inversely due to momentum conservation. From these findings, we propose a $\textit{universal scaling law}$ that relates all key impact loadings to the simple parameter of the droplet $\textit{projection area}$, which can be determined solely from the initial droplet geometry and orientation. This law provides a predictive framework for impact loading dynamics of non-ideal shapes, offering new insights into the mechanisms of LEE and improving the accuracy of erosion predictions for wind turbine blades.

title: Case-Specific Priors-Guided Multimodal Fusion for Prognosis Prediction in Head and Neck Cancer
summary: Accurate prognosis prediction for head and neck cancer typically necessitates integrating highly heterogeneous clinical and pathological evidence by sophisticated multimodal fusion. However, existing fusion techniques are usually grounded in case-generic clinical rationales about complementary synergies across modalities, underestimating case-specific variance. In this study, we propose a prognosis prediction framework that explicitly incorporates Case-specific Priors to guide Multimodal fusion (named CPM). It leverages broad medical knowledge of LLMs to characterize each case's (case-specific) intra-modal contexts and inter-modal relations, as well as case-generic multimodal rationale, as priors, enabling three-stage priors-guided multimodal fusion: (i) Intra-modal Context-guided Calibration (IntraCC) that leverages case-specific intra-modal priors to guide feature calibration within each modality; (ii) Inter-modal Relation-guided Interaction (InterRI) that leverages case-specific inter-modal priors to guide pair-wise feature interaction in modality pairs; and (iii) Multimodal Rationale-guided Aggregation (MultiRA) that leverages case-generic multimodal priors to guide final feature aggregation over all modalities. On the well-established HANCOCK challenge dataset involving four distinct medical modalities, our CPM achieved a mean AUC of 83.98% for predicting 5-year overall survival and 2-year recurrence-free survival, improving upon the baseline by 7.58%, pioneeringly demonstrating the effectiveness of LLM-derived medical priors in guiding multimodal fusion for prognosis prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/yuelin421/CPM.

title: How the elastic axis folds the transonic flutter boundary: shock energy transfer and conformally calibrated active learning
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23415511
summary: Isogai's case A, a pitch-plunge aerofoil whose elastic axis lies half a chord ahead of the leading edge, has a folded transonic flutter boundary in inviscid flow: near the bottom of the transonic dip several flutter speeds coexist at one Mach number. We map this boundary, and the family obtained by moving the elastic axis, with coupled unsteady Euler simulations, a Gaussian-process surrogate of the damping coefficient trained by batch active learning, and split conformal prediction on independent random simulations, which turns the surrogate into stability calls with a distribution-free error rate. Three failure modes of time-domain damping labels that leave no trace in the residuals are documented, and the half-degree mean incidence left by the common one-degree start is shown to raise the flutter speed at the dip by 2.8%, more than any numerical setting. With 80 simulations the learned case A boundary labels 64 of 65 independent runs correctly, and calibrated calls are wrong in at most 1.6% of cases. Over Mach number, elastic axis and flutter speed index, 193 simulations and 40 calibration runs show that the fold exists only for elastic axes more than about 0.4 chord ahead of the leading edge; it closes between 0.39 and 0.33 chord ahead, on two meshes. Chordwise energy budgets, closed against the solver loads and the growth rate within a few per cent, explain the boundary. The lower branch is crossed through the reduced frequency at unchanged shock phase. On the upper branch the shock is pinned at the trailing edge, and moving the elastic axis aft brings the pivot of the flutter mode towards the section, so that the damping of the supersonic surface falls faster than the residual shock input and the fold closes.

title: Really Need Recursion? Revisiting One-pass Registration with Multi-level Multi-space Contextual Guidance
summary: Deformable image registration is a fundamental challenge in medical image analysis. Recent deep learning-based methods typically adopt either one-pass architectures that complete registration in a single network iteration, or recursive architectures that refine registration through multiple passes. While recursive methods often improve accuracy, they incur substantial computational overhead and slower inference speed. In this paper, we challenge the necessity of recursion for high-performance deformable registration and propose M2CG, a one-pass registration network with Multi-level Multi-space Contextual Guidance. It performs multi-step progressive pyramid registration within a single iteration, guided at each step by contextual cues from three levels (previous, current, and subsequent steps) and four spaces (image space, image feature space, segmentation space, and segmentation feature space). Our M2CG supports both unsupervised (without any labels) and semi-supervised (with segmentation labels for partial training data) registration, and has achieved state-of-the-art performance across two well-benchmarked inter-/intra-patient medical registration tasks with eight public datasets. Our findings suggest that the current reliance on recursion may stem from the absence of sufficient contextual cues that comprehensively characterize the remaining distance to the target alignment.

title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology
summary: We present GINNGER (GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for GEnerative Rheology), a framework for discovering thermodynamically admissible constitutive equations from microstructural flow data. Unlike existing approaches that learn constitutive operators, GINNGER reformulates constitutive discovery as the learning of the underlying thermodynamic generators from which constitutive equations emerge. Embedding the GENERIC formalism into the learning process restricts the search to constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction, eliminating the need to prescribe phenomenological constitutive equations a priori. A second conceptual advance is a spectral formulation of constitutive discovery in the intrinsic eigenspace of the polymer conformation tensor. This provides a kinematics-independent thermodynamic state space in which the thermodynamic generators depend only on the instantaneous microstructural state, while flow kinematics acts solely as an external driver transporting the system through this space. Consequently, data from shear, extensional, and mixed flows contribute to the discovery of a single constitutive model that generalizes across deformation protocols and flow geometries. By learning thermodynamic generators rather than high-dimensional constitutive operators, GINNGER substantially reduces the complexity of the discovery problem while preserving thermodynamic consistency, material objectivity, and physical interpretability by construction. The framework is validated using high-fidelity simulations, accurately reconstructing constitutive behavior and predicting complex flow fields across previously unseen geometries. GINNGER establishes a new paradigm for constitutive discovery by combining generative, spectral, and thermodynamically grounded learning within a unified framework for data-driven modeling of complex fluids.

title: Adv-Camou: An Emissivity-based Physical Dynamic Adversarial Patch for Infrared Attack
summary: With the widespread application of infrared object detection technologies in military domains, intelligent infrared adversarial camouflage capabilities have become critical. Existing physical attack methods predominantly employ static thermal suppression strategies, suffering from limited environmental adaptability, insufficient attack robustness, and inadequate visual concealment. This study proposes Adv-Camou, an emissivity-based physical dynamic adversarial patch that achieves paradigm-shifting advancements from static to dynamic attacks through algorithm-material co-innovation. First, a multi-level loss function based on feature confusion mechanisms is designed to deceive detectors by attenuating target saliency and enforcing background feature alignment. Second, adaptive physical transformations and differentiable binarization optimization are integrated to address physical robustness and realizability constraints. A 6*4 array of reversible electrochromic emissivity device is developed and tested across a range of background scenarios, enabling scene-adaptive dynamic camouflage through independent unit control. Experiments demonstrate that this method achieves 95.59% attack success rate (ASR), reducing average precision (AP) by 60.51%. Physical validations show that static adversarial patches attain 76.55% average ASR under multi-view, multi-range, and multi-spectral conditions, while dynamic patches enhance ASR up to 91.55% in complex environments (wilderness/urban) through adaptive switching. The seamless digital-to-physical transfer via tunable emissivity devices transcends the limitations of traditional static camouflage by establishing a dynamic infrared regulation capability. This advancement enhances the battlefield survivability of military assets and demonstrates transformative potential for adaptive camouflage in practical combat scenarios.

title: Hydrodynamics and propulsive efficiency of stern-sculling propulsion
summary: Stern-sculling is a traditional form of human-powered boat propulsion in which a single oar is oscillated laterally at the stern. In this study, we investigate this propulsion technique from a hydrodynamic perspective by continuously measuring the oar kinematics, the boat motion, and the forces acting on the oar across a broad range of boat speeds. During the lateral strokes, lift serves as the main propulsive force, whereas during the backward strokes, propulsion is primarily associated with added-mass effects. These measurements allow us to determine the propulsive efficiency as a function of boat speed. The efficiency peaks at approximately 65\% at an intermediate speed and then decreases progressively to approximately 25\% at higher speeds. These results provide insight into the hydrodynamic mechanisms governing this traditional mode of propulsion and highlight the effectiveness of stern-sculling at moderate speeds.

title: A Unified Theory of Image Scaling: Point Spread Functions, Discrete Kernels, and Scale-Spaces
summary: We derive the optically aligned system of image-scaling operators $\mathbf{K}_s$ that reproduces optical zoom (exact zoom-out, canonical zoom-in), by identifying a Huygens-like consistency principle in which each pixel acts as a secondary source. The system is determined in closed form by the camera's point spread function (PSF), itself the operator $\mathbf{K}_0$. The operators compose, $\mathbf{K}_{s'} \circ \mathbf{K}_s = \mathbf{K}_{ss'}$ (with band projection for down-up), and account for both upscaling and downscaling, which form a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse pair, $\mathbf{K}_{1/s} = \mathbf{K}_s^\dagger$. We show that image scaling, as routinely practiced, is neither optically faithful nor internally consistent; for example, common anti-aliasing rules generally correspond to no camera, and two resizes by a factor of $1/2$ generally do not equal one resize by a factor of $1/4$. Gaussian scale-space kernels cannot be exact finite-aperture PSFs. Gaussian scale-space is an idealized special case of what emerges here: a generalized scale-space for sampled images, derived entirely from camera optics, bidirectional, and not limited to Gaussian kernels. The system goes beyond scaling and supports composable and invertible subpixel geometric transformations. We empirically validate its optical predictions with real captures and noisy optics simulations, and demonstrate its practical impact on the stability of tasks such as super-resolution and classification.

title: Wake effects in a 100 GW North Sea offshore wind scenario: a model intercomparison under year-round weather conditions
summary: Large-scale offshore wind development will intensify wake interactions between wind farm clusters in the North Sea, increasing uncertainty in regional energy estimates. We assess HARMONIE-AROME mesoscale simulations, ASPIRE large-eddy simulations (LES), and three engineering wake models based on Jensen, Bastankhah Gaussian, and TurbOPark formulations for a 100.7 GW 2050 offshore wind scenario. We find that LES and mesoscale simulations accurately represent observed local free-stream wind conditions. Moreover, all engineering wake models predict higher mean wind speeds than LES in every month, with biases reaching 0.60-0.70 m/s at 10-40 km downstream. These differences also vary systematically with atmospheric regime: the Bastankhah Gaussian model remains positively biased across wind speed and stability conditions, whereas Jensen and TurbOPark shift from underprediction in unstable and near-neutral conditions to overprediction in stable conditions at 8-12 m/s. These results show that agreement in annual capacity factor can conceal substantial differences across space, time, and atmospheric regime, highlighting the importance of including sensitivity to model formulation in regional wind energy assessments.

title: LGGS: Longitudinal MRI Reconstruction via Guided Group Sparsity
comment: 10 pages main, 8 figures main, 5 pages supplementary, 7 figures supplementary
summary: Serial MRI is routinely performed in current clinical practice for disease surveillance and applications such as MR-guided radiotherapy. However, long MRI scan times increase costs and limit patient access, making accelerated image reconstruction of broad clinical importance. Previous scans of the same patient contain image information highly correlated with the current exam, yet existing reconstruction methods rarely exploit this information. Major challenges in the effective use of prior scans include inter-visit misregistration, pathological changes, and image phase variation. In this work, we propose Longitudinal Guided Group Sparsity (LGGS), an interpretable deep-learning framework for longitudinally informed MRI reconstruction derived from classical group sparsity. The prior scan is incorporated into the reconstruction regularizer through learned phase-invariant circulant attention that identifies corresponding features across exams. This formulation provides robustness to local in-plane and through-plane misregistration as well as inter-visit phase variation. Across acceleration rates, LGGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on longitudinal T1-weighted multi-coil brain MRI data, outperforming the evaluated unguided and longitudinally informed reconstruction methods, with substantially fewer learned parameters. We further evaluated the contributions of multiple guide slices and phase-invariant similarity and demonstrated that accelerated prior images can also serve as effective guides with minimal degradation in reconstruction quality.

title: Effects of Spanwise Curvature on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition in Görtler-driven Flows
summary: The influence of spanwise convex curvature on hypersonic boundary-layer transition over a streamwise-concave surface is investigated using direct numerical simulation and Mach 7 experiments. Smooth doubly curved geometries with fixed streamwise concavity and increasing spanwise convex curvature isolate the effects of three-dimensional wall curvature on a centrifugally unstable boundary layer. Increasing spanwise curvature delays transition while preserving a Gortler-dominated route to breakdown. As spanwise curvature increases, the boundary layer thins, reducing the effective Görtler number and weakening centrifugal amplification of streamwise vortices. Consequently, growth of the primary Görtler instability is reduced, vortical structures remain closer to the wall, and secondary instability and turbulent breakdown shift downstream. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition confirms that low-frequency vortical dynamics remain dominant in controlling transition, with sinuous secondary instability of Görtler vortices providing the principal route to breakdown. Meanwhile, boundary-layer thinning modifies acoustic instability dynamics: the second Mack mode shifts to higher frequencies and higher-frequency supersonic disturbances become increasingly prominent near breakdown as spanwise curvature increases. These acoustic disturbances remain subdominant and do not replace the Görtler-sinuous mechanism as the primary transition pathway. Numerical and experimental results exhibit consistent trends in transition location, thermal-streak organisation and disturbance evolution, supporting a common physical interpretation. These findings demonstrate that spanwise convex curvature stabilises hypersonic Görtler-dominated boundary layers, primarily by suppressing centrifugal amplification and delaying secondary instability, while leaving the transition pathway qualitatively unchanged.

title: Image Moment Estimation for Crowded Datasets
summary: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is an imaging technique capable of reconstructing high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) structure of biological macromolecules from a set of noisy projection images taken at random viewing directions. The mathematical model for cryo-EM images typically assumes that each image contains exactly one particle, which is centered at the origin. However, many experimental datasets contain particle images which include multiple particles: one central particle and a few crowding particles. This deviation from the model leads to inaccurate estimation of image statistics, such as the low-order image moments. To account for this, we propose a method to estimate image moments while correcting for the effect of crowding particles. This method can be run directly from a set of cryo-EM micrographs with picked particles, and we demonstrate its efficacy on a wide array of synthetic data.

title: The typical red cell makes too little vacuole material for coalescence to build the large vacuoles of pocked cells
comment: 70 pages, 8 figures; Supplementary Materials included (pages 36-70, 2 figures, 28 tables); Movies S1 and S2 are ancillary files. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Red blood cells carrying intracellular vacuoles, called pocked cells, are a sensitive marker of splenic function: about 0.5% of cells in healthy people, 20 to 70% after splenectomy. Vacuoles too small to see are common, and visible ones are thought to grow when small ones merge. We tested that idea with a particle model that resolves the cell's membrane, its contents and every vacuole, and with an inventory of the vacuole volume a cell can make. In tube, shear and vascular flows, a cell's vacuoles met within a second, and, allowed to fuse, ten merged into one to five. Meeting is not what limits growth; material is. At the rate measured after splenectomy, all the vacuoles an average cell makes in its 120-day life fuse into one body 0.6 $μ$m across, the size healthy cells carry, but 16 times smaller in volume than the 1.5-$μ$m bodies of patients without a spleen. Taking vacuole size as set at formation, a population model in which vacuoles are made mainly in young cells, and far faster in a small minority that alone makes material for a large one, accounts for the published counts, sizes and age profiles and, on first-hand measurements, favours a splenic clearance that rises several-fold as cells age; letting that minority's vacuoles fuse fits nearly as well. At a model splenic slit, the cell's spare surface decided passage, and a vacuole mattered only when it led. A slit experiment would test whether brief encounters fuse vacuoles.

title: Measurement-Adaptive Light-Cone Transform for Robust Non-Line-of-Sight Imaging
summary: Practical non-line-of-sight (NLOS) measurements are affected by noise and deviations from idealized light transport, which can degrade reconstruction with conventional light-cone transform (LCT) methods. We propose the Measurement-Adaptive Light-Cone Transform (MALCT), a physics-guided framework that retains the efficient Fourier-domain inversion structure of LCT. {Within a unified variational formulation, MALCT combines the analytical response with a shared learned response through measurement-conditioned weighting and predicts a measurement-conditioned, frequency-dependent regularization map.} An attention-enhanced spatio-temporal feature extraction module captures long-range temporal dependencies and local spatial correlations to support reconstruction under low-signal conditions. Experiments on synthetic data and real measurements from different NLOS systems demonstrate improved reconstruction quality. Controlled evaluations further assess robustness to temporal-response broadening and reduced acquisition time. MALCT also preserves scene structures with spatial sampling grids down to $32\times32$, supporting its potential for NLOS imaging under limited acquisition budgets.

title: Stabilizing Illumination Conditioning in SSM-Based Low-Light Image Enhancement with Bottleneck Prompt Sidecars
summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) requires more than brightness amplification because real low-light images often exhibit spatially varying illumination, amplified noise, color distortion, and local detail loss. Recent SSM- and Mamba-based restorers provide efficient long-range modeling, yet the route for introducing illumination priors into such backbones remains insufficiently studied. This study addresses safe illumination conditioning for SSM-based LLIE through a bottleneck-side PromptAdapter. A lightweight illumination estimator first predicts a single-channel illumination map, which is then converted into prompt tokens and injected through a residual sidecar adapter at the bottleneck, thereby avoiding direct modification of the state-space core. Under a locked three-seed evaluation protocol on LOL-v1, LOLv2-Real, and LOLv2-Synthetic, the PromptAdapter improves over the Base model by 0.94 dB, 1.24 dB, and 0.93 dB in PSNR, respectively, while also improving SSIM, LPIPS, and masked dark-region metrics. The clearest real-data evidence appears on LOLv2-Real. A Learned-Fixed control on LOL-v1 indicates that the present results support the utility of the sidecar conditioning pathway more strongly than a strict claim of illumination-conditioned superiority, and the LOLv2-Synthetic result remains stability-conditioned. These findings suggest that, in SSM-based LLIE, conditioning design can be as important as the conditioning signal itself.

title: Spatiotemporal Adaptive Eigenspectrum Remapping in Transcranial Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
summary: Clutter suppression is a critical preprocessing step in ultrasound blood flow imaging, yet conventional singular value decomposition (SVD) filtering depends on data-specific eigenvalue cutoffs that can remove slow flow along with tissue clutter. Here, we introduce adaptive eigenspectrum remapping (AER), a general framework in which clutter is suppressed by continuously remapping, rather than truncating, the eigenvalue spectrum of the spatiotemporal covariance, and we investigate zero-phase component analysis (ZCA) matrix whitening as an instance of AER for transcranial ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM). Rather than discarding eigenspaces, ZCA-based AER whitens the eigenvalue spectrum, reducing the dominance of coherent clutter, including skull reverberation, while retaining weak flow signals. We evaluate AER on both temporal and spatial covariance matrices in mouse brain datasets acquired with long temporal ensembles. Compared with SVD filtering, ZCA improves microbubble contrast and vascular image quality, increases trajectory density across low- and high-concentration regimes, and reveals more low-velocity trajectories in ULM velocity maps. Spatial AER further maintains reconstruction quality across extended ensembles and enables fuller single capillary reporter (SCaRe) reconstructions, including connected artery-to-capillary-to-vein tracks. These results support AER, here instantiated as ZCA whitening, as a data-adaptive alternative to manually thresholded SVD filtering for high-resolution microvascular imaging.

title: TransNSNet: A Transformer-Enhanced Multi-Scale Adversarial Framework for CT-to-PET Image Synthesis
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures. Supplementary material included. Under review at Biomedical Signal Processing and Control
summary: This study investigates CT-to-PET image synthesis using TransNSNet, a Transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework. A paired CT-PET dataset was curated from the public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) Radiogenomics collection through patient screening, slice-level matching, preprocessing, and patient-level train-test separation. The proposed framework generates PET-like predictions at multiple spatial scales and applies coarse-to-fine reconstruction supervision, while TransPatchGAN introduces contextual feature interaction into adversarial evaluation. A progressive ablation study compares Pix2Pix, NSNet-Base, NSNet-D, and TransNSNet. Image-level performance was summarized over a fixed convergence window (epochs 80-101) from one training run per model. TransNSNet achieved the best mean value in nine of ten metrics, whereas NSNet-Base achieved the highest visual saliency-induced index. For fixed-fraction high-intensity regions, NSNet-D was marginally higher in slice-level recall and balanced accuracy, but the equal-weight patient-level values were nearly identical and the highest Dice values shifted to TransNSNet. These differences were small relative to between-patient variability. In the separate adaptive patient-level analysis (n=10), no pairwise model difference remained statistically significant after Holm correction. TransNSNet also had a substantially smaller parameter footprint than the original next-scale models. These findings indicate promising image-quality trends, but they do not establish statistical superiority or clinical validity; synthesized PET-like images should not be interpreted as substitutes for clinically acquired PET.
